paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems that encourage sparse solutions through explicit constraints. Both the objective and the sparsity constraints can be nonconvex, making the resulting problem difficult to solve directly. The proposed model accommodates a range of continuous sparsity constraints rather than committing to a single form.

The algorithm breaks the original problem into a sequence of convex subproblems. Each combines a proximal objective, which anchors the update to a reference point, with a convex replacement for the constraint. The constraint levels are gradually relaxed. A fast projection routine makes these intermediate problems efficient to solve, providing a practical route through the harder overall problem.

The authors prove convergence to solutions satisfying the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and give complexity guarantees for reaching approximate versions of those conditions. These cover several objective settings, including stochastic and nonsmooth ones, with complexities comparable to corresponding unconstrained gradient-descent results. The guarantees concern KKT solutions, rather than global optimality. Numerical experiments support the method’s effectiveness on large problems.
neurips-2020-a-feasible-level-proximal-p.tldr: A proximal algorithm solves nonconvex sparse-constrained problems through convex subproblems, with convergence and complexity guarantees for approximate KKT solutions.

paragraphs: AViD is a public action-recognition dataset designed around geographical diversity. Its motivation is that training videos drawn mainly from a few countries may prepare models unevenly for videos from elsewhere. The paper examines this concern and finds that most existing video datasets are statistically concentrated in a limited set of countries.

The dataset collects action videos from many countries, anonymizes face identities, and provides a static collection whose videos carry Creative Commons licenses. These choices combine broader geographical coverage with privacy protection and a fixed collection for training. The contribution therefore concerns how the data is assembled and made available, as well as its usefulness for recognizing actions.

Experiments show that models trained on geographically concentrated datasets transfer imperfectly to videos from other countries, and that AViD addresses this problem. The authors also evaluate its value for pretraining, reporting performance comparable to or better than prior datasets. These findings support broader country coverage as a useful consideration when building action-recognition training resources.
neurips-2020-avid-dataset-anonymized-vid.tldr: AViD offers anonymized action videos from diverse countries and shows benefits for cross-country transfer and model pretraining.

paragraphs: Multiclass classifiers often train with a surrogate loss because directly minimizing classification mistakes is difficult. A surrogate can have favorable Bayes-consistency properties while behaving poorly when its scoring functions are restricted. This paper examines why such guarantees may fail to deliver the best classifier within a particular model class, the concern addressed by H-consistency.

The authors show that the choice of scoring functions is central to this issue. For one-vs-all hinge and logistic losses, they derive scoring-function classes that enable H-consistency in the realizable setting considered. The implication is that a failure with one natural scoring class need not rule out the surrogate itself; a more carefully designed class can remedy the problem.

For linear classifier models, the proposed scores are certain piecewise linear functions with the same parameter count as standard linear scores. Training uses an adaptation of min-pooling. Experiments find that these nonlinear scores produce better linear multiclass classifiers than training the same surrogates with ordinary linear scores.
neurips-2020-bayes-consistency-vs-h-cons.tldr: Carefully chosen nonlinear scoring functions can restore H-consistency for particular surrogates and improve the linear multiclass classifiers they produce.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised object detection trains with labels saying which categories occur in an image, without labels specifying object locations. This leaves considerable ambiguity: a detector may focus on a distinctive part, favor a particularly salient object, or group nearby objects together. Category labels also do not directly require predictions to remain consistent across transformed versions of an image.

Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation addresses these issues by combining attention information from multiple transformations and feature layers of the same image. This aggregated attention is intended to balance feature learning across object instances. It provides a shared spatial target assembled from several views of the network’s own information.

The method then trains multiple transformations and feature layers to approximate that common attention target. This self-distillation step supplies more consistent spatial supervision while retaining image-level labeling. The authors report new state-of-the-art weakly supervised detection results on PASCAL VOC 2007, PASCAL VOC 2012, and MS-COCO, supporting the usefulness of combining attention aggregation with consistency during training.
neurips-2020-comprehensive-attention-sel.tldr: CASD aggregates attention across image transformations and network layers to improve object detection trained only with image-level labels.

paragraphs: Momentum-based optimization has a useful connection to physical motion with friction. Nesterov’s accelerated gradient and Polyak’s heavy ball can be understood as different discrete versions of a second-order differential equation. This paper uses that connection to investigate how properties of continuous dynamics carry over into practical optimization updates.

The authors study discretizations that preserve structure in a class of dissipative Hamiltonian systems. This gives them a framework for examining the symplectic structure of both Nesterov and heavy ball. The focus is on the mathematical organization of the updates, offering another way to understand acceleration through their relationship with underlying dynamical systems.

The paper also proposes an optimizer derived from a dissipative relativistic system. Its momentum is normalized, which may improve stability or speed. Both Nesterov and heavy ball arise as distinct limiting cases, so the construction connects the established methods within a broader family. The stated advantages are potential ones, available without additional cost, rather than an unconditional claim of faster optimization.
neurips-2020-conformal-symplectic-and-re.tldr: A structure-preserving dynamical-systems analysis leads to a momentum-normalizing optimizer that generalizes Nesterov and heavy ball and may improve stability or speed.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes that could lead to a favorable decision. People may act strategically on this advice, investing effort to improve their chances. This paper treats those reactions as part of the design problem: which explanations, and which decision policy, yield the best utility when people respond to them?

For a fixed policy, selecting the optimal explanation set is NP-hard. However, the objective is nondecreasing and submodular, meaning additional explanations have diminishing returns. That structure gives a standard greedy algorithm approximation guarantees. When the policy and explanations are selected jointly, the authors instead obtain a non-monotone submodular problem and apply a randomized algorithm with approximation guarantees.

The formulation can also include a matroid constraint to encourage a more diverse explanation set and incentives for self-improvement across the population. Experiments using synthetic data and real lending and credit-card data illustrate the theoretical results. In those evaluations, the proposed policies and explanations achieve higher utility than several competitive baselines.
neurips-2020-decisions-counterfactual-ex.tldr: The paper designs decision policies and counterfactual explanations around strategic responses, using submodular optimization to obtain approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: An intervention in a social system can change how self-interested participants behave. A designer therefore needs to anticipate those responses, which depend on payoff functions that may be unknown. This paper connects learning about participants with choosing interventions, placing both within one end-to-end optimization framework.

The central construction treats a game’s equilibrium as a layer through which training gradients can pass. Equilibria are represented as solutions of variational inequalities. One differentiation approach explicitly unrolls the projection-based procedure used to solve those inequalities. The other differentiates implicitly, using how their solutions respond to changes in the problem.

Both approaches depend on differentiating through a projection operator. The authors establish their correctness and identify conditions favoring one approach over the other, rather than presenting a single universally preferable method. They validate the analytical results on several real-world problems. The framework matters because it incorporates anticipated equilibrium behavior directly into the learning and intervention process, linking the designer’s choices to participants’ reactions.
neurips-2020-end-to-end-learning-and-int.tldr: Differentiable game-equilibrium layers connect learning participants’ payoffs with optimizing interventions that account for their responses.

paragraphs: Many selection problems combine diminishing returns with a budget: recommendations, team formation, and viral marketing are examples discussed here. The objective may also be non-monotone, so adding an item can reduce value. This paper targets the computational difficulty of solving such problems at large scale, including settings with stochastic outcomes.

The authors propose a randomized greedy algorithm for submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint. It achieves a 5.83 approximation and runs in O(n log n) time. The stated running time is at least a factor of n faster than other state-of-the-art algorithms, addressing the cost of applying existing methods to massive instances.

The approach also extends to a stochastic version, where decisions can adapt as information becomes available. There it gives a 9-approximation to the best adaptive policy, which the authors identify as the first constant approximation for non-monotone objectives. Experiments on real and synthetic data show improved performance, complementing the theoretical tradeoff between efficient computation and solution quality.
neurips-2020-fast-adaptive-non-monotone-.tldr: A fast randomized greedy method provides approximation guarantees for budgeted non-monotone submodular selection and an adaptive stochastic extension.

paragraphs: This paper tackles abstract visual reasoning when only a small amount of training data is available. Its starting point is analogical reasoning: recognizing that different problems share a relational structure. The aim is to learn representations of those relationships so that training examples teach more than the appearance of individual puzzles.

Training uses pairs of problem instances that are either analogous or non-analogous. Non-analogous examples can be created by perturbing or shuffling an original problem. A contrastive objective encourages representations of analogous pairs to be similar while reducing similarity for non-analogous pairs. This makes the relationship between problems an explicit source of supervision.

On RAVEN, the method outperforms the state-of-the-art method considered, with larger gains when training data is scarce. The authors also meta-learn the model across the same tasks with varied attributes and demonstrate transfer to unseen attributes of the same visual reasoning problem. That result supports generalization across attributes within the studied problem, rather than a claim of unrestricted reasoning transfer.
neurips-2020-few-shot-visual-reasoning-w.tldr: Contrastive learning between analogous visual puzzles improves few-shot reasoning, while meta-learning supports transfer to unseen attributes of the same problem.

paragraphs: Q-learning can overestimate action values because its updates rely on random samples. Double Q-learning addresses this issue using two value estimators and randomly choosing which one to update. Although the method was already popular in practice, its established convergence theory described eventual behavior without specifying how quickly useful accuracy could be reached.

This paper provides a finite-time analysis for both synchronous and asynchronous double Q-learning. It bounds the iterations sufficient to reach an epsilon-accurate neighborhood of the global optimum. The bound depends on the desired accuracy, the discount factor, and the parameter controlling how quickly the learning rate decreases.

Those dependencies make the guarantee more informative than eventual convergence alone: they connect an accuracy target to an iteration requirement. The proof also develops techniques for controlling the difference between two coupled stochastic processes, reflecting the interaction between the estimators. The contribution is therefore both a convergence-rate guarantee for double Q-learning and a way to analyze intertwined random update processes.
neurips-2020-finite-time-analysis-for-do.tldr: The paper gives finite-time convergence guarantees for synchronous and asynchronous double Q-learning by analyzing its two coupled estimators.

paragraphs: Generating new videos from a single training video requires producing variation from very limited evidence. Existing hierarchical patch-GAN approaches had shown promise for single-image generation, but their extension to video often produced little diversity. Outputs could collapse toward samples resembling the training video, undermining the goal of generating novel examples.

The paper introduces a patch-based variational autoencoder and uses it within a hierarchical generation process. At coarse scales, this patch-VAE supplies diversity. At finer scales, a patch-GAN adds visual detail. The design assigns different roles to the two components, using one to create varied samples and the other to refine their appearance.

Experiments demonstrate diverse generation in both images and videos, with video identified as the more challenging setting. The stated result supports combining coarse-scale variation with fine-scale rendering when training from one sample. The contribution is especially relevant to the tension highlighted by the paper: a generator can reproduce a source convincingly while still failing to produce meaningfully varied outputs.
neurips-2020-hierarchical-patch-vae-gan-.tldr: A hierarchical generator combines a coarse-scale patch-VAE with a fine-scale patch-GAN to produce diverse videos from one training sample.

paragraphs: This paper focuses on the gradient computations used to train neural ordinary differential equation models. It proposes a simple interpolation-based method for approximating those gradients efficiently. The intended benefit is faster training through a different gradient-computation procedure, making this step of the learning process the central object of study.

The comparison is with the reverse dynamic method, also known as the adjoint method. The authors evaluate both approaches on classification, density estimation, and inference approximation tasks. Studying these different uses lets them examine the proposed procedure across several kinds of neural ODE training rather than relying on a single application.

The paper also offers a theoretical justification using logarithmic norm formalism, alongside extensive numerical experiments on several standard benchmarks. Those experiments confirm faster training than the reverse dynamic method in the evaluated settings. The resulting contribution connects an interpolation-based gradient approximation with both mathematical support and observed training-speed benefits; the empirical comparison is specifically against the stated adjoint approach.
neurips-2020-interpolation-technique-to-.tldr: An interpolation-based gradient approximation speeds neural ODE training relative to the adjoint method in the reported benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Event cameras provide precise timing, low data rates, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for motion, difficult lighting, and low-latency applications. Yet event-based object detection has faced gaps in sensor resolution, training data, and established architectures. This paper addresses all three through a dataset and a recurrent detection model.

The dataset contains more than 14 hours of automotive recordings from a one-megapixel event camera, with 25 million bounding boxes for cars, pedestrians, and two-wheelers. The detector uses internal memory to compactly represent event sequences and adds a temporal consistency loss for training. The authors identify this memory as essential to achieving high accuracy.

The recurrent model substantially outperforms feed-forward event-based architectures in the reported experiments. It also processes events without reconstructing intensity images, which the authors find more efficient and accurate than that intermediate route. On their dataset, where events and grayscale images are both available, detection performance matches that of highly tuned frame-based detectors.
neurips-2020-learning-to-detect-objects-.tldr: A large automotive event dataset and recurrent detector achieve frame-detector-level performance on the introduced dataset while learning directly from events.

paragraphs: Running a nonlinear recurrent neural network across T steps ordinarily takes time proportional to T. LDStack seeks to shorten the parallel computation by approximating that network with a stack of linear dynamical systems. Its key move is to relocate nonlinearity from the progression through time to the progression through network depth.

The construction first approximates the recurrent network with multiple-input, multiple-output linear systems. It then approximates those systems using averages or concatenations of single-input, multiple-output systems. An algorithm can execute and differentiate the latter in O(log T) parallel time. The authors state that repetition can make the approximation error arbitrarily small.

Experiments on long sequences find LDStack much faster than traditional recurrent networks while achieving similar accuracy. The logarithmic claim concerns parallel time, which is the computational measure used by the construction. Beyond speed, the use of linear systems makes the model accessible to linear systems theory, providing a basis for the claimed improvements in interpretability and mathematical tractability.
neurips-2020-linear-dynamical-systems-as.tldr: LDStack approximates nonlinear recurrent networks with stacked linear dynamical systems that support execution and differentiation in logarithmic parallel time.

paragraphs: Certifiable training aims to produce networks whose robustness can be verified, but existing approaches can be slow or difficult to scale. This paper develops a training algorithm combining Lipschitz analysis with interval arithmetic. Its central device is box constraint propagation, or BCP, which produces a tight outer bound during propagation through the network.

The algorithm efficiently computes the worst logit over this outer bound, making the bound useful during training. Experiments find that BCP gives a tighter bound than the global Lipschitz-based alternative. A tighter bound matters because the certification calculation depends on the set of possibilities enclosed by that bound.

The authors report training more than twelve times faster than the state-of-the-art dual relaxation-based method considered, with comparable or better verification performance and improved natural accuracy. They also scale to Tiny ImageNet, obtaining 20.1% verification accuracy for an l2 perturbation radius of 36/255. These results connect the proposed bounding procedure to both computational efficiency and demonstrated certification performance.
neurips-2020-lipschitz-certifiable-train.tldr: Box constraint propagation enables faster certifiable training with tighter bounds and competitive verification performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: MPNet addresses two issues in language-model pretraining. BERT’s masked language modeling neglects dependencies among the tokens being predicted. XLNet’s permuted language modeling captures those dependencies, but does not use the sentence’s full positional information, creating a discrepancy between pretraining and fine-tuning. The paper combines ideas from both approaches.

MPNet uses permuted language modeling to account for relationships among predicted tokens. It also supplies auxiliary positional information so that the model has access to the full sentence’s position structure. These two components address different aspects of the training objective: how target predictions depend on one another, and what positional context is available while making them.

The authors pretrain on more than 160 GB of text and fine-tune on tasks including GLUE and SQuAD. Their experiments report large gains over masked and permuted language modeling, as well as better results than BERT, XLNet, and RoBERTa under the same model setting. The findings support the combined objective within those controlled model comparisons.
neurips-2020-mpnet-masked-and-permuted-p.tldr: MPNet combines dependencies among predicted tokens with full positional information to improve language understanding in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Previous results established that online learnability and private PAC learnability coincide for binary classification. This paper asks how far that connection extends when predictions involve multiple classes or numerical values. The question is whether the existence of a learner in one setting also guarantees the existence of a learner in the other.

The authors prove that private learnability implies online learnability for both multiclass classification and regression. Their analysis introduces a tolerance-dependent variant of the Littlestone dimension and generalizes threshold functions beyond binary classification. These tools allow the relationship to be studied in settings where the original binary formulation is insufficient.

For multiclass classification, they also prove the reverse implication, establishing equivalence. Regression remains unresolved in the reverse direction: current proof techniques face significant obstacles. The paper nevertheless gives nontrivial sufficient conditions under which an online-learnable regression class is also privately learnable. Those conditions establish positive cases without settling equivalence for regression as a whole.
neurips-2020-on-the-equivalence-between-.tldr: Online and private learnability are equivalent for multiclass classification, while regression receives one implication and sufficient conditions for the unresolved reverse direction.

paragraphs: The paper studies learners that output a data-dependent distribution over hypotheses and use that distribution for randomized predictions. The central question is how well those predictions generalize beyond the finite training sample. PAC-Bayes analysis addresses this by bounding the predictor’s expected risk on unseen examples.

The authors present a basic PAC-Bayes inequality for stochastic kernels, from which existing bounds can be extended and new ones derived. They distinguish the underlying inequality from assumptions commonly used to turn it into particular bounds. Specifically, data-independent priors, bounded losses, and independent identically distributed data have been used to control an exponential moment term.

The basic theorem remains valid without those restrictions, although controlling that term is still part of deriving a useful bound. The authors illustrate the framework with three bounds involving data-dependent priors, including one for unbounded squared loss. The contribution clarifies which assumptions belong to the general theorem and which enter particular ways of evaluating its terms.
neurips-2020-pac-bayes-analysis-beyond-t.tldr: A general PAC-Bayes inequality separates the core theorem from familiar assumptions and supports bounds with data-dependent priors and unbounded squared loss.

paragraphs: Biological networks must compute despite noisy neurons, variable connections, and communication delays. Averaging across N neurons conventionally reduces coding error like 1/sqrt(N). Earlier work showed that recurrent spiking networks using predictive coding and tightly balanced inputs and feedback could instead achieve 1/N scaling. This paper investigates the principles behind that stronger scaling.

The authors introduce a tractable model in which the degree of balance can vary independently of disorder in connection weights. This separation matters because it allows the effects of cancellation and connectivity variability to be examined individually. They develop a mean-field theory describing coding accuracy within the model.

The resulting framework analyzes how neural noise, weight disorder, chaos, delays, and balance contribute to the fidelity of predictive codes. It reveals the fundamental role of balance in achieving the stronger scaling and connects previously separate theoretical neuroscience models. The contribution is an analytical account of these interacting influences, providing a way to study reliability beyond simple averaging across neurons.
neurips-2020-predictive-coding-in-balanc.tldr: A tractable theory separates balance from connection disorder to explain their roles in predictive coding accuracy amid noise, chaos, and delays.

paragraphs: Learning systems may need explicit behavioral requirements alongside predictive accuracy, particularly in sensitive applications. This paper builds a generalization theory for such constrained learning using the probably approximately correct framework. It asks whether learning with requirements remains possible and how a learner can enforce them from finite data.

The authors show that any PAC-learnable class is also PAC constrained learnable through a constrained version of empirical risk minimization. This is a learnability result, while implementation presents a separate challenge. For typical parameterized models, the required optimization is constrained and nonconvex, and even finding a feasible solution can be difficult.

To address that computational obstacle, the paper proves that, under mild conditions, an empirical dual formulation is also a PAC constrained learner. This leads to an algorithm based on solving unconstrained problems. The authors analyze its generalization and illustrate applications to fair and robust classification. The framework therefore connects statistical guarantees for requirements with a more practical way to optimize under them.
neurips-2020-probably-approximately-corr.tldr: A PAC theory establishes constrained learnability and, under mild conditions, supports a practical dual algorithm built from unconstrained optimization.

paragraphs: Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis seeks a discriminative subspace for representing data. This paper changes the mathematical formulation used to compute that subspace, replacing the original trace-ratio problem with a ratio-trace problem. The closely related names conceal a consequential change: the reformulation supports a different approach to optimization.

The proposed algorithm uses an eigensolver and is presented as an efficient, more stable alternative to the original gradient-based method. The authors also supply a rigorous convergence analysis within the self-consistent field framework. This adds theoretical support for the computation, addressing a convergence-analysis gap identified in the earlier literature.

The paper applies the learned representation to subspace clustering by combining WDA with low-dimensional clustering methods such as K-means. Numerical experiments on real datasets show promising results for both classification and clustering. Together, these contributions connect a reformulated objective, an analyzed numerical algorithm, and downstream uses of the resulting subspace, while keeping the empirical claim at the level of promising observed performance.
neurips-2020-ratio-trace-formulation-of-.tldr: A ratio-trace reformulation gives Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis an eigensolver-based algorithm with convergence analysis and promising classification and clustering results.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks without losing what it learned earlier. Much of the work motivating this paper focused on feed-forward classification networks. The authors instead study recurrent LSTM models for image captioning, where learning sequential tasks involves generating descriptions with vocabularies that can overlap.

Their method, Recurrent Attention to Transient Tasks, explicitly accommodates that vocabulary overlap through an attention-based approach. Shared words mean task vocabularies cannot simply be treated as separate sets. The paper also adapts weight-regularization and knowledge-distillation methods to recurrent continual learning, creating a broader investigation of approaches for this setting.

The authors define two continual image-captioning benchmarks using MS-COCO and Flickr30. In their reported results, RATT learns five captioning tasks sequentially without forgetting previously learned tasks. That finding establishes the demonstrated behavior on these benchmarks, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary task sequences. The work expands continual-learning evaluation to recurrent language generation grounded in images and highlights overlapping vocabularies as a design concern.
neurips-2020-ratt-recurrent-attention-to.tldr: RATT uses attention to accommodate overlapping captioning vocabularies and learns five tasks without observed forgetting on the proposed benchmarks.

paragraphs: An agent may receive information beyond the transition caused by its chosen action. Auxiliary sensors or prior knowledge can provide additional transition samples, including information about actions with similar outcomes. This paper studies how such side observations can improve learning in tabular Markov decision processes.

The authors represent observation relationships with a feedback graph over state-action pairs. Model-based algorithms then incorporate the extra samples into learning. Their regret bound depends predominantly on the size of a maximum acyclic subgraph, shifting the main complexity measure toward the structure of available feedback rather than the usual polynomial dependence on state and action counts.

The paper also examines whether a small dominating set in the graph can help an agent gather useful information efficiently. It identifies fundamental challenges that distinguish this setting from bandit problems, then proposes an algorithm that can exploit such a set to learn a near-optimal policy faster. The results show how both the availability and arrangement of side observations matter.
neurips-2020-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Feedback graphs let model-based reinforcement learning exploit extra transition observations, with guarantees tied to the graph’s structure.

paragraphs: Reservoir computing uses a recurrent network with fixed random internal weights and trains only a linear output layer. This makes training simple, but the size of the random network still affects computation and memory. The paper develops two alternatives by connecting large reservoirs to kernel methods and structured random features.

First, the authors rigorously establish a recurrent-kernel limit and prove convergence to it. On chaotic time-series prediction, the resulting Recurrent Kernel method is competitive and computationally efficient when the number of data points is moderate. This connects a limiting mathematical description of the random network to a usable prediction method.

For larger sample counts, the authors introduce Structured Reservoir Computing, drawing on structured random features used in kernel approximation. The two approaches therefore address different data-size regimes within the same broader connection. Both are reported to be much faster and more memory-efficient than conventional reservoir computing. The moderate-data qualification is central to the stated efficiency of the direct recurrent-kernel approach.
neurips-2020-reservoir-computing-meets-r.tldr: A proven recurrent-kernel limit and a structured-reservoir alternative improve the speed and memory efficiency of reservoir computing.

paragraphs: Zap Q-learning is a family of reinforcement-learning algorithms motivated by faster convergence. Its stability theory had been restricted to tabular problems and optimal stopping. This paper extends the analytical treatment to nonlinear function approximation, addressing a setting that includes neural-network representations of action values.

The authors first develop a framework for analyzing stochastic approximation, a broader class of recursive algorithms. They use that theory to prove consistency of Zap Q-learning under a non-degeneracy assumption, even with nonlinear approximators. The assumption is part of the guarantee, so the result does not establish unconditional consistency for every nonlinear architecture or problem.

Neural-network Zap Q-learning appears as a special case and is evaluated on OpenAI Gym examples. Across experiments with different network sizes, the algorithms converge quickly and show robustness to the choice of approximation architecture. The paper thus pairs a conditional theoretical extension with empirical evidence across several network configurations, broadening the support for Zap Q-learning beyond its previously analyzed settings.
neurips-2020-zap-q-learning-with-nonline.tldr: Zap Q-learning gains a consistency guarantee for nonlinear approximation under a non-degeneracy assumption, alongside promising neural-network experiments.
